The effect of possible in-medium modifications of nucleon-nucleon ($NN$) cross sections on particle production is investigated in heavy ion collisions ($HIC$) at intermediate energies. In particular, using a fully covariant relativistic transport approach, we see that the density dependence of the {\it inelastic} cross sections appreciably affects the pion and kaon yields and their rapidity distributions. However, the $(\pi^{-}/\pi^{+})$- and $(K^{0}/K^{+})$-ratios depend only moderately on the in-medium behavior of the inelastic cross sections. This is particularly true for kaon yield ratios, since kaons are more uniformly produced in high density regions. Kaon potentials are also suitably evaluated in two schemes, a chiral perturbative approach and an effective meson-quark coupling method, with consistent results showing a similar repulsive contribution for $K^{+}$ and $K^{0}$. As a consequence we expect rather reduced effects on the yield ratios. We conclude that particle ratios appear to be robust observables for probing the nuclear equation of state ($EoS$) at high baryon density and, particularly, its isovector sector.

# In-Medium Cross Section Effects on Particle Production in Heavy-Ion Collisions

## Theoretical Framework and Motivation

The present study employs a fully covariant relativistic transport approach to systematically investigate how in-medium modifications of nucleon-nucleon cross sections influence particle production dynamics in heavy ion collisions at intermediate energies. Unlike simplified treatments that rely on free-space cross sections, this covariant framework self-consistently incorporates the density-dependent nature of hadronic interactions within the dense nuclear medium created during the collision process. This approach is particularly well-suited for probing the properties of nuclear matter under extreme conditions, since intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions provide a unique terrestrial environment for compressing nuclear matter to several times normal nuclear density, conditions otherwise inaccessible in laboratory settings.

## Density Dependence of Inelastic Cross Sections

A central finding of this work is that the density dependence of inelastic nucleon-nucleon cross sections exerts a significant influence on both pion and kaon production yields, as well as on their respective rapidity distributions. Since pions and kaons are predominantly produced through inelastic channels—via baryon resonance excitation and subsequent decay for pions, and through associated strangeness production processes for kaons—the manner in which these cross sections evolve with local baryon density directly shapes the space-time evolution of particle emission. Modifications to the in-medium cross sections alter the effective production thresholds and reaction rates at different stages of the collision, thereby redistributing the yields across the accessible rapidity range and affecting the total multiplicities of these mesonic species. This sensitivity underscores the importance of accurately modeling the medium dependence of elementary cross sections when interpreting experimental particle spectra from heavy-ion collision experiments.

## Stability of Particle Ratios

In contrast to the individual yields, the ratios of oppositely charged and isospin-partner mesons—specifically the (π⁻/π⁺) and (K⁰/K⁺) ratios—display only moderate sensitivity to the in-medium behavior of the inelastic cross sections. This relative insensitivity arises because many of the density-dependent effects that modify the absolute production rates tend to cancel when forming these ratios, as both species in each pair are subject to similar medium modifications during their production and propagation through the collision zone. Notably, the kaon ratios exhibit an even greater degree of stability compared to the pion ratios. This enhanced robustness can be attributed to the fact that kaons, given their higher production threshold and characteristic emission time profile, are predominantly generated during the early, high-density phase of the collision, resulting in a more spatially uniform production pattern across the compressed nuclear medium. Consequently, local fluctuations or density-dependent variations in the cross sections have a diminished net effect on the K⁰/K⁺ ratio compared to pions, which are copiously produced throughout all stages of the reaction, including the lower-density expansion phase.

## Consistency of Kaon In-Medium Potentials

To further substantiate the robustness of the kaon ratio as an observable, the kaon in-medium potentials were evaluated using two independent theoretical frameworks: a chiral perturbative approach, grounded in effective chiral Lagrangians that describe the low-energy interactions between kaons and the nuclear medium, and an effective meson-quark coupling model, which describes kaon-nucleon interactions at the level of constituent quark degrees of freedom. Despite their differing theoretical foundations, both approaches yield consistent results, predicting similar repulsive potential contributions for both K⁺ and K⁰ mesons within the nuclear medium. Because these repulsive potentials act comparably on both kaon species, their effect on the overall production dynamics is largely symmetric, which further diminishes any residual influence of the in-medium cross sections on the K⁰/K⁺ yield ratio. This cross-validation between two distinct theoretical descriptions lends additional confidence to the reliability of the calculated kaon potentials and their role in shaping observable ratios.

## Implications for Nuclear Equation of State Studies

Taken together, these findings establish particle yield ratios—particularly the K⁰/K⁺ ratio—as robust and reliable observables for probing the properties of the nuclear equation of state at high baryon densities. Because such ratios are largely insensitive to uncertainties in the in-medium behavior of inelastic cross sections, they offer a cleaner and more direct window into the underlying density-dependent nuclear interactions, especially the isovector (symmetry energy) sector of the equation of state. This is of particular significance for ongoing efforts to constrain the high-density behavior of the nuclear symmetry energy, a quantity of fundamental importance not only for understanding heavy-ion collision dynamics but also for astrophysical applications such as neutron star structure and the physics of core-collapse supernovae. The demonstrated stability of these particle ratios against variations in the treatment of in-medium cross sections thus strengthens their utility as diagnostic tools in future experimental and theoretical investigations of dense nuclear matter.

# In-Medium Cross Sections and Particle Production in Heavy Ion Collisions: Probing the Nuclear Equation of State

## Introduction

The study of heavy ion collisions at intermediate energies (typically 0.1–2 GeV/nucleon) provides a unique terrestrial laboratory for probing the properties of nuclear matter under extreme conditions of density, temperature, and isospin asymmetry. Of particular interest is the behavior of the nuclear equation of state (EoS) at supra-saturation densities, and especially its isovector component—the symmetry energy—which remains poorly constrained despite its critical importance for understanding neutron star structure, supernova dynamics, and the physics of neutron-rich nuclei. Heavy ion collisions offer a controlled environment in which dense, isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter is transiently created, making them an essential tool for constraining the density dependence of the symmetry energy.

Among the various observables proposed to extract information about the EoS from heavy ion collision data, particle production—particularly of pions and kaons—has attracted considerable attention. Pions, being copiously produced in these reactions, are sensitive to the isospin asymmetry of the participant matter through the isospin-dependent nucleon-nucleon (NN) and nucleon-Delta (NΔ) interactions. Kaons, on the other hand, being produced primarily in the early, high-density phase of the collision through inelastic NN and pion-baryon collisions, serve as a cleaner probe of the compressed nuclear matter due to their long mean free path and the absence of strong final-state interactions with the surrounding hadronic medium.

However, the reliability of these observables as EoS probes hinges critically on our understanding and proper treatment of two closely related but often underappreciated effects: (1) the in-medium modification of nucleon-nucleon cross sections, both elastic and inelastic, and (2) the in-medium properties of the produced kaons themselves, namely their potential energy in the nuclear medium. Both of these ingredients introduce significant theoretical uncertainties into transport model calculations, potentially obscuring the extraction of EoS parameters from experimental data.

## Motivation and Scope

Nucleon-nucleon cross sections used as inputs to transport simulations are typically taken from free-space, vacuum measurements. However, it has long been recognized that the nuclear medium can substantially modify these cross sections due to Pauli blocking, the modification of the nucleon effective mass, and the screening of the interaction by the surrounding nucleons. This is particularly relevant for inelastic channels responsible for pion and kaon production, such as NN → NΔ, NN → NN* , and NN → NNK+Y (Y=Λ,Σ), since these channels feed directly into the calculated meson yields.

Simultaneously, the propagation of kaons through the dense nuclear medium is governed by their in-medium potential, which arises from the interaction between the strange quark content of the kaon and the surrounding nucleons. Two theoretical frameworks have been widely employed to derive this potential: chiral perturbation theory (ChPT), which treats the kaon as a pseudo-Goldstone boson of spontaneously broken chiral symmetry and predicts a repulsive K+ potential and attractive K− potential, and effective meson-quark coupling models based on relativistic mean-field theory, which describe the kaon-nucleon interaction through the exchange of scalar and vector mesons coupled to the light quarks within the kaon.

This study aims to systematically investigate the interplay between these two physical ingredients—in-medium NN cross sections and kaon in-medium potentials—within a unified covariant relativistic transport framework, and to assess their combined impact on pion and kaon production, as well as on isospin-sensitive particle ratios such as π⁻/π⁺ and K⁰/K⁺.

## Theoretical Framework

The calculations presented here are performed within a relativistic transport model based on the covariant relativistic Vlasov-Uehling-Uhlenbeck (RVUU) or Boltzmann-Uehling-Uhlenbeck (RBUU) approach, in which the nucleons, deltas, and produced mesons are propagated according to relativistic mean-field equations of motion derived from an effective Lagrangian (such as the non-linear Walecka model or its density-dependent extensions). This framework self-consistently incorporates the isovector channel through the ρ-meson field, allowing for a controlled variation of the symmetry energy stiffness.

The in-medium modification of the nucleon-nucleon cross section is implemented through a density- and momentum-dependent scaling of both the total and channel-resolved (elastic and inelastic) cross sections relative to their free-space values. Several parameterizations are explored, ranging from cross sections that decrease with increasing baryon density (motivated by Brueckner-Hartree-Fock calculations and Dirac-Brueckner approaches) to cross sections that remain closer to their free-space values, allowing an assessment of the sensitivity of the results to this poorly constrained input.

For the kaon sector, two distinct approaches to the in-medium potential are implemented and compared:

1. **Chiral perturbation theory approach**: The kaon self-energy is derived from the leading-order chiral Lagrangian, including the Tomozawa-Weinberg term and next-to-leading order corrections from scalar meson exchange, yielding a repulsive K+ potential of the order of 20-40 MeV at saturation density.

2. **Effective meson-quark coupling approach**: The kaon is treated as a composite quark-antiquark state, with its light quark(s) coupling to the scalar (σ) and vector (ω, ρ) meson fields of the surrounding nuclear medium in the same manner as the nucleon's constituent quarks, leading to a potential whose density and isospin dependence can differ appreciably from the ChPT prediction, especially in isospin-asymmetric matter.

## Results and Discussion

The simulations are carried out for a range of heavy ion collision systems (e.g., Au+Au, Sn+Sn) at beam energies spanning approximately 0.4 to 1.5 GeV/nucleon, and for different impact parameter selections, in order to sample a broad range of baryon densities and isospin asymmetries reached in the collision.

The results demonstrate that the density dependence of the inelastic NN cross sections has a substantial quantitative effect on the absolute yields of both pions and kaons. Softer (more strongly density-suppressed) inelastic cross sections lead to reduced production of Δ resonances and consequently lower pion multiplicities, as well as reduced kaon yields due to the suppressed feeding through NΔ and NN* channels. The magnitude of this effect can reach factors of order unity in the absolute particle yields, comparable to or even exceeding the sensitivity to the choice of kaon potential model.

Similarly, the choice between the chiral perturbative and meson-quark coupling kaon potentials produces visible differences in the kaon excitation function and its dependence on beam energy, with the meson-quark coupling model generally predicting a somewhat different density dependence of the K+ potential, particularly at the higher densities probed by more energetic or more central collisions.

Despite these substantial effects on the absolute particle yields, the ratios of isospin partner mesons—π⁻/π⁺ and K⁰/K⁺—are found to be remarkably insensitive to both the treatment of the in-medium NN cross sections and the choice of kaon potential model. This robustness arises because both the numerator and denominator of these ratios are affected in a very similar manner by these medium modifications: since the cross-section suppression and kaon potential effects act nearly symmetrically on both isospin partners (to the extent that isospin-symmetric medium effects dominate over isospin-splitting effects), the ratio largely cancels out these systematic uncertainties.

This cancellation confirms and reinforces the theoretical expectation that isospin-sensitive particle ratios represent a comparatively "clean" observable for constraining the isovector part of the nuclear equation of state, in contrast to absolute yields which are subject to substantial theoretical uncertainty stemming from poorly known aspects of the reaction dynamics such as in-medium cross sections and meson potentials.

## Conclusions

This study has systematically examined the influence of in-medium nucleon-nucleon cross section modifications and kaon in-medium potentials—evaluated using both chiral perturbative and effective meson-quark coupling frameworks—on pion and kaon production in heavy ion collisions at intermediate energies, within a covariant relativistic transport approach. While the absolute yields of pions and kaons are found to be significantly affected by the density dependence of the inelastic cross sections, as well as by the choice of kaon potential model, the isospin-sensitive ratios π⁻/π⁺ and K⁰/K⁺ remain remarkably stable against these variations.

These findings provide important validation for the continued use of particle ratio observables in extracting information about the density dependence of the symmetry energy at supra-saturation densities from heavy ion collision data, while simultaneously highlighting the need for improved theoretical and experimental constraints on in-medium cross sections and meson potentials in order to reliably interpret absolute particle production yields. Future work should focus on further disentangling these effects through differential observables, such as transverse momentum and rapidity distributions of the particle ratios, which may offer additional leverage in constraining both the isoscalar and isovector components of the nuclear equation of state at densities relevant to neutron star physics.

# Hydrophobic Interaction Chromatography (HIC)

**The** purification of proteins is a critical step in biotechnology and pharmaceutical manufacturing, and among the various separation techniques available, Hydrophobic Interaction Chromatography (**HIC**) stands out as a particularly valuable method. This technique separates biomolecules based on their surface hydrophobicity, exploiting the reversible interaction between hydrophobic patches on protein surfaces and hydrophobic ligands attached to a chromatographic resin.

**The** process typically begins by loading a protein sample onto the HIC column in a high-salt buffer. Under these conditions, salt ions promote the exposure of hydrophobic regions on the protein surface, encouraging binding to the hydrophobic stationary phase. This phenomenon, known as "salting-out," is fundamental to how HIC achieves selective separation. As the salt concentration in the mobile phase is gradually decreased, proteins elute from the column in order of increasing hydrophobicity—those with the least hydrophobic surfaces elute first, while more hydrophobic proteins require lower salt concentrations to be released.

One of the primary advantages of **HIC** is its compatibility with proteins in their native, biologically active conformations. Unlike some other purification methods that require harsh chemical conditions, HIC operates under relatively mild conditions, making it especially suitable for purifying sensitive biopharmaceuticals such as monoclonal antibodies, enzymes, and other therapeutic proteins.

**However**, HIC is not without its limitations. The technique requires careful optimization of buffer conditions, salt type, and gradient parameters to achieve optimal resolution. Additionally, some proteins may exhibit irreversible binding or aggregation under high-salt conditions, potentially leading to sample loss or reduced yield. **However**, when properly optimized, HIC often complements other chromatographic techniques such as ion-exchange or size-exclusion chromatography, providing an additional dimension of selectivity in multi-step purification protocols.

In conclusion, despite these challenges, HIC remains an indispensable tool in the biopharmaceutical industry, offering a gentle yet effective means of protein purification that preserves biological activity while achieving high purity standards.

# Abstract

We investigate the influence of in-medium modifications of nucleon-nucleon (NN) cross sections on the production of pions and kaons in relativistic heavy-ion collisions using a covariant transport model based on the relativistic Boltzmann-Uehling-Uhlenbeck (RBUU) approach. The elementary NN elastic and inelastic (pion-production) cross sections entering the collision integral are commonly taken from free-space scattering data; however, at the high baryon densities and temperatures reached in heavy-ion collisions, these cross sections are expected to be modified due to Pauli blocking, short-range correlations, and the effective in-medium masses and coupling constants dictated by the underlying relativistic mean-field dynamics. In this work, we implement density- and momentum-dependent in-medium NN cross sections, derived self-consistently from the same effective Lagrangian used to generate the mean fields, and compare the resulting particle production yields, spectra, and flow observables with calculations employing free-space cross sections.

Our results show that in-medium suppression of the NN cross sections leads to a sizable reduction in the number of NN collisions above the pion-production threshold, thereby suppressing pion multiplicities, while simultaneously softening the transverse and rapidity distributions due to reduced rescattering. The effect on kaon production is more subtle: although the primary NN → NΛK channel is also suppressed by the reduced elementary cross section, the enhanced stopping power and higher compression achieved in the in-medium scenario partially compensate for this suppression, leading to a smaller net change in the total kaon yield compared to pions. We further explore secondary effects on strangeness-exchange reactions and pion/kaon collective flow, finding that in-medium cross-section modifications noticeably affect the sensitivity of these observables to the nuclear equation of state at supra-normal densities.

These findings emphasize the importance of consistently treating in-medium cross sections alongside mean-field potentials in covariant transport simulations, and demonstrate that pion and kaon yields and flow patterns provide complementary and sensitive probes for constraining both the nuclear equation of state and the density dependence of hadronic cross sections in the dense medium created in heavy-ion collisions. Comparisons with existing SIS/AGS energy data are used to test the consistency of the in-medium cross-section parametrization and to place constraints on the high-density behavior of NN interactions relevant for astrophysical applications such as neutron star matter.

# Abstract

The nuclear equation of state (EOS) at supra-saturation densities remains one of the most challenging open problems in nuclear physics, with direct implications for heavy-ion collision dynamics and neutron star structure. Kaon and pion production in heavy-ion collisions provides a unique experimental window into this regime, as their yields and ratios are sensitive to the density-dependent symmetry energy and the in-medium properties of strange and non-strange mesons. In this work, we investigate kaon-to-pion yield ratios, specifically K+/π+ and K0/π+ (or their charged and neutral combinations), as sensitive probes of the nuclear EOS at densities of 2-3 times saturation density, achievable in heavy-ion collisions at intermediate energies (1-2 AGeV).

We employ a transport model framework incorporating in-medium kaon potentials derived from two complementary theoretical approaches: chiral perturbation theory (ChPT) and the quark-meson coupling (QMC) model. The ChPT-based approach treats kaons as pseudo-Goldstone bosons within an effective chiral Lagrangian, generating repulsive K+ and attractive K- potentials through leading-order and next-to-leading-order interaction terms with the nuclear medium. In contrast, the QMC model describes kaon-nucleon interactions through the coupling of light quarks to scalar and vector meson fields within the MIT bag model framework, providing an alternative microscopic picture of medium modifications. We systematically compare the density and momentum dependence of kaon optical potentials predicted by both approaches and examine their consequent impact on kaon production yields and ratios in central heavy-ion collisions.

Our calculations demonstrate that the double ratio [K+/K0]_{Au+Au}/[K+/K0]_{C+C} or similar isospin-sensitive observables exhibit significant sensitivity to both the nuclear symmetry energy and the choice of kaon potential, while showing reduced sensitivity to the compressibility of symmetric nuclear matter compared to single kaon yields. We find that the ChPT and QMC approaches, despite differing microscopic origins, yield qualitatively similar density dependencies for the K+ potential at moderate densities, though noticeable differences emerge at higher densities relevant to compact astrophysical objects. The pion yield ratios, particularly π-/π+, provide complementary constraints on the symmetry energy through the Coulomb-corrected isospin diffusion mechanism. Combined analysis of kaon and pion observables offers enhanced discriminating power for constraining the density-dependent symmetry energy and the EOS stiffness, with direct relevance to predictions of neutron star maximum mass and radius. These results underscore the complementary role of strangeness production as an independent probe of nuclear matter properties, providing essential input for bridging terrestrial heavy-ion experiments with astrophysical observations of dense nuclear matter.

**Keywords:** nuclear equation of state, kaon production, symmetry energy, chiral perturbation theory, quark-meson coupling model, heavy-ion collisions, neutron star constraints

# Abstract

The influence of medium modifications to inelastic nucleon-nucleon (NN) cross sections on particle production and isospin observables in heavy-ion collisions at intermediate energies (200 MeV/nucleon – 2 GeV/nucleon) is investigated within a microscopic transport model framework. While in-medium corrections to elastic NN cross sections have been extensively studied, the density and momentum dependence of inelastic channels—governing pion, delta resonance, and strangeness production—remains comparatively underconstrained despite their pivotal role in interpreting heavy-ion observables as probes of the nuclear equation of state (EOS) and its isospin-dependent components.

We implement a set of density-dependent parametrizations for inelastic NN cross sections, motivated by Brueckner-Hartree-Fock and effective field theory calculations, and examine their impact on pion multiplicities, the π⁻/π⁺ ratio, delta resonance yields, and strangeness (K⁺/K⁰) production in Au+Au and Sn+Sn collisions across the considered energy range. Our results demonstrate that in-medium suppression of the inelastic cross section at high baryon density reduces overall pion yields while simultaneously reshaping the isospin-sensitive π⁻/π⁺ and K⁰/K⁺ ratios, introducing a sensitivity to the density dependence of the symmetry energy at supra-saturation densities that is comparable to, and partially entangled with, the effect of the mean-field potential itself.

We further show that this cross-section dependence propagates into transverse momentum spectra and rapidity distributions of produced particles, affecting extracted freeze-out conditions and complicating direct EOS extraction from pion ratios alone. A systematic comparison with available data from FOPI, HADES, and S$\pi$RIT collaborations constrains the allowed range of in-medium suppression factors and highlights the necessity of disentangling cross-section-driven effects from genuine EOS signatures. These findings underscore that reliable determination of the symmetry energy at high density requires simultaneous, correlated treatment of both mean-field dynamics and in-medium two-body collision rates, and they provide guidance for reducing systematic uncertainties in transport model comparisons used to constrain the neutron-rich nuclear EOS.

# Robustness of π⁻/π⁺ and K⁰/K⁺ Ratios as Isovector EOS Probes

## Background and Motivation

Heavy-ion collisions at intermediate to high energies compress nuclear matter to several times saturation density, creating conditions where the density dependence of the symmetry energy (the isovector part of the nuclear equation of state) can, in principle, be probed. Since the symmetry energy at supra-saturation densities remains poorly constrained by nuclear structure data, meson production ratios sensitive to the neutron-to-proton excess of the participant region have been proposed as sensitive observables.

## Key Findings from Relativistic Transport Studies

**1. Pion Ratios (π⁻/π⁺) Show Significant Model Dependence**

- The π⁻/π⁺ ratio, particularly at high transverse momentum or high kinetic energy, was historically proposed as a sensitive probe of the high-density symmetry energy (softer vs. stiffer forms).
- However, systematic comparisons across different relativistic transport codes (and between transport approaches, e.g., RBUU-type vs. others) reveal that the extracted symmetry energy stiffness depends strongly on:
  - Treatment of the pion potential/self-energy in the medium
  - Threshold effects and in-medium modifications of the Δ resonance
  - Momentum-dependent interactions and isospin-dependent mean fields for nucleons and resonances
  - Numerical treatment of pion absorption/rescattering
- These sensitivities lead to **large spreads in predicted π⁻/π⁺ ratios** for a given symmetry energy parameterization, undermining the reliability of pion ratios as a clean, model-independent constraint. Different codes can give qualitatively opposite trends (softer symmetry energy giving either enhanced or suppressed ratios) depending on implementation details of the reaction dynamics rather than the symmetry energy itself.

**2. Kaon Ratios (K⁰/K⁺) Demonstrate Greater Robustness**

- The K⁰/K⁺ ratio (or related strangeness ratios) is less contaminated by resonance/threshold ambiguities because kaons are produced with smaller cross sections at higher threshold energies, primarily through more elementary and better-constrained production channels (e.g., BB → BYK, πB → YK).
- Kaons undergo negligible reabsorption after production (small K-N cross section), so the ratio largely reflects conditions at production—directly tied to the local neutron/proton density asymmetry at the moment of high-density compression.
- Transport calculations across different codes show **much better agreement** in the correlation between K⁰/K⁺ and the symmetry energy slope, making it a more trustworthy tool.
- The K⁰/K⁺ excitation function is comparatively less sensitive to in-medium mean-field ambiguities of the pion sector and to details of Δ resonance dynamics, thus offering more consistent constraints on the density dependence of the symmetry energy across models.

## Overall Conclusions

- **Pion ratios**, despite their historical appeal (higher production yield, easier to measure), suffer from significant transport-model dependence due to intertwined sensitivities to the symmetry energy, the pion/Δ in-medium potentials, and threshold effects — reducing their reliability as quantitative EOS constraints without further code convergence.
- **Kaon ratios**, though statistically more challenging to measure due to lower yields, emerge as the **more robust and trustworthy observable** for constraining the high-density symmetry energy, since they are less entangled with uncertain in-medium pion/Δ physics and are dominated by production-stage isospin asymmetry rather than final-state interactions.
- This has motivated increased experimental and theoretical emphasis on strangeness (K⁰/K⁺) measurements alongside continued efforts to better constrain and cross-validate pion-sector physics in transport codes (e.g., through community code-comparison exercises) before pion observables can be reliably used for symmetry-energy extraction.

# In-Medium Effects on Kaon Production and Collective Flow in Heavy-Ion Collisions

## Abstract

The dynamics of strangeness production in heavy-ion collisions provides a sensitive probe of nuclear matter properties under extreme conditions of density and temperature. In this study, we investigate the influence of in-medium nucleon-nucleon (NN) cross sections and kaon-nucleon potentials on particle yields, ratios, and collective flow observables in heavy-ion collisions at intermediate energies, employing a transport-theoretical framework based on the Boltzmann-Uehling-Uhlenbeck (BUU) equation.

We systematically compare two classes of kaon in-medium potentials: those derived from chiral effective Lagrangian approaches, which incorporate the Weinberg-Tomozawa interaction term and scalar meson exchange contributions, against potentials obtained from meson-quark coupling models that treat the kaon's internal quark structure explicitly through medium-modified quark condensates. These approaches yield qualitatively similar attractive (K⁻) and repulsive (K⁺) potentials at nuclear saturation density but differ in their density dependence and momentum-dependent behavior, particularly at supra-normal densities reached in the compressed collision zone.

Complementing this, we examine the impact of density- and energy-dependent in-medium NN cross sections, evaluated using Dirac-Brueckner-Hartree-Fock calculations and Cugnon parametrizations, as opposed to free-space cross sections. Our results demonstrate that in-medium cross sections significantly affect the collision rate, the equilibration timescale, and consequently the total kaon multiplicity, while the choice of kaon potential predominantly governs the K⁺/K⁻ ratio and the differential flow patterns of these mesons relative to nucleon flow.

Calculations performed for Au+Au collisions at SIS energies (1-2 A GeV) show that the combined interplay between the nuclear equation of state stiffness, the in-medium cross sections, and the kaon potential scheme produces distinct, experimentally distinguishable signatures in the excitation function of the K⁺/K⁻ ratio and in the kaon flow correlations. We find that chiral-motivated potentials tend to produce a more pronounced squeeze-out signal for K⁻ mesons due to their stronger density dependence, while meson-quark coupling potentials predict a softer transverse flow response. These findings are benchmarked against data from the FOPI, KaoS, and HADES collaborations, allowing us to place constraints on the strangeness sector of the nuclear equation of state and to disentangle the competing contributions of two-body dynamics (cross sections) from mean-field effects (potentials) in dense nuclear matter.

Our analysis underscores the necessity of simultaneously constraining both in-medium cross sections and kaon potentials to reliably extract information about the high-density nuclear equation of state from heavy-ion collision observables, offering guidance for future high-precision measurements at FAIR and NICA facilities.
